learn.intro: Emancipation freed about four million people. Reconstruction brought citizenship, the vote and black officeholders — and then a violent backlash and the federal government's retreat in 1877. Section B questions often compare this period with 1883–c1900 or 1933–45.

sections.title: 1. The Thirteenth Amendment and the realities of freedom

blocks.p: The Thirteenth Amendment (ratified December 1865) abolished slavery throughout the United States, except as punishment for a crime. About four million people were freed.

Economic position: freedpeople wanted land. General Sherman's Field Order No. 15 (January 1865) set aside coastal land in South Carolina and Georgia for black families, but President Andrew Johnson restored most confiscated land to former owners in 1865. Without land or capital, most freedpeople became wage labourers or sharecroppers — farming a landowner's land for a share of the crop — and the crop-lien system tied them to debt with local merchants.
Freedom of movement mattered enormously: people travelled to find family members separated by sale, moved to towns, and left plantations. Black churches became independent centres of community life.

Education: the Freedmen's Bureau (March 1865), northern missionary societies and black communities themselves set up schools; colleges such as Fisk (1866) and Howard (1867) were founded. Literacy was valued as a mark of freedom. White Southerners often met these changes with hostility and violence.

sections.title: 2. Johnson's response and the political settlement

blocks.p: Andrew Johnson, a Southern Democrat who became President after Lincoln's assassination in April 1865, offered lenient terms: pardons for most Confederates, and readmission once states abolished slavery and renounced secession. He showed no interest in black political rights.

Southern legislatures passed Black Codes (1865–66) — for example in Mississippi and South Carolina — controlling black workers through vagrancy laws, annual labour contracts and restrictions on property and movement. Johnson vetoed the renewal of the Freedmen's Bureau and the Civil Rights Act of 1866; Congress overrode him. Riots in Memphis and New Orleans in 1866 killed dozens of black people and turned northern opinion towards the Radical Republicans in the 1866 elections.

evidence: 1866: Civil Rights Act passed over Johnson's veto.

sections.title: 3. Radical Reconstruction, 1867–77

blocks.p: The Reconstruction Acts (1867) divided ten southern states into five military districts and required them to write new constitutions with black male suffrage and to ratify the Fourteenth Amendment before readmission. Johnson's opposition led to his impeachment (1868); he was acquitted by one vote.

The Fourteenth Amendment (1868) made all people born in the USA citizens and promised 'equal protection of the laws'. The Fifteenth Amendment (1870) banned denying the vote on grounds of 'race, color, or previous condition of servitude'. The Enforcement Acts (1870–71), including the Ku Klux Klan Act, let President Grant use federal force; in 1871 he suspended habeas corpus in parts of South Carolina. The Civil Rights Act of 1875 banned discrimination in public accommodations.

Black Americans held office in large numbers for the first time: Hiram Revels (1870) and Blanche K. Bruce (1875) of Mississippi sat in the US Senate, black representatives sat in Congress, and hundreds served in state legislatures. Their presence showed what political rights could achieve — and provoked fierce white resistance.

evidence: 1870: Fifteenth Amendment; Hiram Revels enters the Senate.

sections.title: 4. The backlash and the end of Reconstruction

blocks.p: The Ku Klux Klan, founded in Tennessee in 1865–66, used terror against black voters, officeholders, teachers and their white allies. After the Enforcement Acts weakened the Klan, paramilitary groups such as the White League in Louisiana (1874) and the Red Shirts acted openly. At Colfax, Louisiana (April 1873), dozens of black men were massacred after a disputed election.

Northern commitment faded: the economic depression after the Panic of 1873, corruption scandals and racism made voters tired of Reconstruction. The Supreme Court narrowed federal protection in the Slaughterhouse Cases (1873) and US v Cruikshank (1876). Democrats 'redeemed' one southern state after another, using violence and fraud, as in the 'Mississippi Plan' of 1875.

The disputed presidential election of 1876 was resolved by the Compromise of 1877: Republican Rutherford B. Hayes became President and the last federal troops were withdrawn from the South. Reconstruction ended, leaving the amendments on paper but black rights in the South largely unprotected.

evidence.q: Give precise evidence of black political gains in Reconstruction.
evidence.model: Hiram Revels (1870) and Blanche K. Bruce (1875) sat in the US Senate; black representatives sat in Congress and hundreds in state legislatures, after the Fifteenth Amendment (1870).

evidence.q: Give precise evidence of the federal retreat from Reconstruction.
evidence.model: The Slaughterhouse Cases (1873) and US v Cruikshank (1876) narrowed federal protection; the Compromise of 1877 withdrew the last federal troops.

flashcards.q: How did the economic position of ex-slaves change after 1865?
flashcards.a: Free but landless: most became wage labourers or sharecroppers, often trapped in debt by the crop-lien system.

flashcards.q: Give two social opportunities of freedom.
flashcards.a: Reuniting families; independent black churches; schools and colleges; freedom to move.

flashcards.q: Why did Johnson's policies anger Radical Republicans?
flashcards.a: Lenient pardons, no black rights, tolerance of Black Codes, vetoes of the Freedmen's Bureau and Civil Rights Act 1866.

flashcards.q: What was the significance of black officeholders in Reconstruction?
flashcards.a: Proved black political participation was possible and effective; provoked violent white backlash.

flashcards.q: How did Grant fight the Klan?
flashcards.a: Enforcement Acts and the Klan Act (1871); suspended habeas corpus in parts of South Carolina; federal prosecutions.
White violence (Klan, White League); northern fatigue after the Panic of 1873; Supreme Court rulings; Compromise of 1877.
White Democrats regaining control of southern states, often by violence and fraud.

flashcards.q: What did the Civil Rights Act of 1875 promise?
flashcards.a: Equal access to inns, public transport and theatres — struck down by the Supreme Court in 1883.

checklist.text: I can explain the reasons for, and impact of, the Thirteenth Amendment, including sharecropping.
I can explain the social and educational opportunities of freedom and the tensions they caused.
I can assess Johnson's response and the need for a political settlement.
I can assess the significance of the Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments, the 1875 Act and black officeholders.
I can judge the impact of the Klan, the White League and Democrat 'Redemption' on the end of Reconstruction.
